claim: The field filter in contractless mode is inverted: `field.IsReadOnly && !field.IsConst` picks readonly fields and skips writable ones. Public mutable fields of T are never serialized, which breaks the requirement's contractless behaviour over public members. Public readonly fields are selected and marked IsWritable: true, so the generated Deserialize assigns to them and Project B fails to compile (CS0191).

claim: Acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' is not implemented. Collect always builds members either contractless (no surrogate) or from the surrogate, and never reads [MessagePackObject], [Key], [IgnoreMember] or [DataContract]/[DataMember] on T. A referenced type with [IgnoreMember] members still has them serialized under name keys. Its int-keyed contract is replaced by string keys, so the wire format differs from what the dynamic/standard resolver produces for the same type.

claim: The field filter in `IsPublicReadWrite` is inverted: it reads `field.IsReadOnly && !field.IsConst` instead of `!field.IsReadOnly`. In contractless mode an ordinary mutable field such as `public int MutableField;` is silently dropped from the wire format. A `public readonly int ReadOnlyField;` is selected instead and gets `IsWritable: true`. The generated Deserialize then assigns the readonly field, so the consuming project fails to compile (CS0191). The same filter makes surrogate mode reject mutable fields with MsgPack022 and accept readonly ones.

Types with only a parameterized constructor or get-only properties get no formatter, and a required or init-only property may produce uncompilable output. The documented 'public read-write' limit makes this partly intended.

claim: IsPublicReadWrite treats public fields as eligible only when field.IsReadOnly is true (inverted). Writable public fields are skipped, and readonly fields are marked IsWritable: true. The generated deserializer then assigns to readonly fields, so the generated formatter will fail to compile (CS0191) or the contractless contract will silently drop data. The inversion is not a security issue by itself, but it is a correctness defect in deserialization of untrusted data shape.

claim: In contractless mode, string-key members are sorted by name and given an IntKey of their index, but isIntKey=false. That is fine, but surrogate int keys with gaps (e.g. 0 and 1000) pass an attacker-irrelevant but unbounded IntKey into the array-layout templates. The array-header size is derived from the max key, so a very large [Key(int.MaxValue)] on a surrogate would make generated code allocate or write a huge array header. Deserialization of an array of that declared length then loops over attacker-supplied header counts; the existing MessagePackSecurity and collection checks do not apply to the generated object formatter's header count.

claim: The generated formatter is emitted as `partial class` with no accessibility modifier. In the existing template the generated formatter is also registered in the source-generated resolver. A user's `public partial class` merges fine, but if the user class is nested or has `sealed`/`static`/other modifiers that differ from the emitted ones, nothing is emitted that preserves them. The generated file also drops type constraints for the formatter class, which is harmless. Because the class is also listed in the resolver, the resolver may now start returning the formatter for T in existing projects. Without opting in, an existing project that happens to add the attribute changes formatter selection for T, which is the intended opt-in.
